column9: Which choice correctly matches each particle to its charge?
column14: Proton: negative, Neutron: positive, Electron: no charge
column15: Proton: no charge, Neutron: negative, Electron: positive
column16: Proton: positive, Neutron: no charge, Electron: negative
column17: Proton: positive, Neutron: negative, Electron: no charge
column28: Protons are positive, neutrons have no charge (neutral), and electrons are negative.

column9: Which particles are found in the nucleus?
column17: Electrons only
column28: The nucleus holds the protons and neutrons. Electrons move around the outside of the nucleus.

column9: What is the overall charge of the nucleus?
column15: Neutral, because the neutrons cancel out the protons
column16: It has no charge because it is so small
column17: Positive, because it contains protons and the neutrons have no charge
column28: The nucleus holds positive protons and neutral neutrons, so its overall charge is positive. Neutrons do not cancel anything out.

column9: How do the masses of the three particles compare?
column15: The proton and the neutron are both about 1 amu; the electron is almost nothing
column16: The electron is the heaviest of the three
column17: The proton and the electron are both about 1 amu; the neutron is almost nothing
column28: Protons and neutrons are each about 1 amu. An electron is about 1/1836 of that, so it adds almost no mass.

column9: Most of the space inside an atom is…
column17: Filled with protons
column28: The nucleus is tiny compared with the whole atom, so an atom is mostly empty space. The gold foil experiment showed this.

column9: Which statement about the Bohr model is TRUE?
column14: The atom is a solid sphere
column15: Electrons travel on fixed energy levels around the nucleus
column17: Electrons are spread evenly through a positive blob
column28: In the Bohr model, electrons travel in fixed orbits (energy levels) around the nucleus. A solid sphere is Dalton's model and a positive blob is the plum pudding model.

column9: A model gets replaced when…
column14: Students find it too hard to draw
column15: New evidence turns up that the old model cannot explain
column17: A more famous scientist writes a new one
column28: Scientists change a model when a new experiment gives evidence the old model cannot explain, like the gold foil experiment did for the plum pudding model.

column9: Why was the plum pudding model replaced by the nuclear model?
column14: It was drawn before the periodic table existed
column16: It could not explain why some alpha particles bounced back — a spread-out positive blob has nothing dense enough to do that
column17: It said atoms could be split, which is wrong
column28: In the gold foil experiment a few alpha particles bounced straight back. Only a small, dense, positive center (a nucleus) could do that, so the nuclear model replaced plum pudding.

column9: The atomic number of an element tells you…
column17: How many energy levels it uses
column28: The atomic number is the number of protons. Every atom of that element has that many protons.

column9: hydrogen-3 — how many protons and how many neutrons?
column17: 1 protons, 2 neutrons
column28: Hydrogen's atomic number is 1, so 1 proton. Neutrons = mass number − protons = 3 − 1 = 2.

column9: carbon-14 — how many neutrons?
column28: Carbon has 6 protons. Neutrons = 14 − 6 = 8.

column9: How many electrons does a neutral atom of Al have?
column28: Aluminum's atomic number is 13. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons: 13.

column9: What is the mass number of hydrogen-3?
column28: The number in the name is the mass number: hydrogen-3 has a mass number of 3.

column9: An element has two isotopes: mass 35 (75% of atoms) and mass 37 (25%). What is its average atomic mass?
column28: Multiply each mass by its share and add: 35 × 0.75 + 37 × 0.25 = 26.25 + 9.25 = 35.5 amu.

column9: An atom is electrically neutral. That means…
column17: It has no charged particles at all
column28: Neutral means the positive and negative charges balance, so the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

column9: A Cl ion has a charge of -1. How many protons does it have?
column28: Gaining or losing electrons never changes the protons. Chlorine's atomic number is 17, so it has 17 protons (and 18 electrons as a −1 ion).

column9: Iron is a…
column17: Neither — it is a compound, not an element
column28: Iron (Fe) is on the left side of the staircase line in the transition metals, so it is a metal.

column9: Which period is P in?
column28: Phosphorus (P) is in the third row of the periodic table, so it is in period 3.

column9: Which description fits the halogens?
column14: Group 1 — very reactive metals with 1 valence electron
column15: Group 17 — very reactive nonmetals with 7 valence electrons
column16: Group 2 — reactive metals with 2 valence electrons
column17: Groups 3–12 — the metals in the middle block
column28: The halogens are group 17: very reactive nonmetals with 7 valence electrons. Group 1 is the alkali metals and group 2 the alkaline earth metals.

column9: Two elements are in the same group. What can you predict?
column14: One must be a metal and one a nonmetal
column15: They will have the same mass
column16: They will be in the same period
column17: They will react in similar ways
column28: Elements in the same group (column) have the same number of valence electrons, so they react in similar ways.

column9: Boron is in group ___ and period ___.
column17: group 13, period 3
column28: Groups are columns and periods are rows. Boron (B) is in column 13 and row 2.

column9: Copper is which family, and is it a metal or a nonmetal?
column17: Alkali metals · Nonmetal
column28: Copper (Cu) is in group 11, in the middle block, so it is a transition metal, and all transition metals are metals.

column9: Which element belongs to the alkaline earth metals?
column17: potassium
column28: The alkaline earth metals are group 2. Magnesium (Mg) is in group 2; potassium is group 1, and sulfur and oxygen are nonmetals in group 16.

column9: Which symbol stands for sodium?
column17: Si
column28: Sodium's symbol is Na, from its Latin name natrium.

column9: An atom has the arrangement 2, 8, 1. What element is it and what does it want to do?
column17: Sodium — lose 1 electron
column28: 2 + 8 + 1 = 11 electrons, so it is sodium. With only 1 valence electron, it is easier to lose that one than gain 7.

column9: How many electrons fit on the third energy level for the elements you draw (1–20)?
column28: For elements 1–20, the levels fill 2, then 8, then 8. The third level holds 8.

column9: Why do elements in group 17 all behave alike?
column14: They all have the same mass number
column15: They each have 7 valence electrons, so they all want one more
column17: They all have full outer levels
column28: Group 17 elements all have 7 valence electrons, so each one wants to gain 1 more to fill its outer level. Same valence electrons means similar behavior.

column9: In a Bohr model of C, how many electrons are on the FIRST ring?
column28: Carbon has 6 electrons: 2 on the first ring (it holds only 2) and 4 on the second.

column9: A Bohr model is drawn with the rings 2, 6. How many electrons is that in total?
column28: Add the rings: 2 + 6 = 8 electrons (that is oxygen).

column9: Draw the Bohr model for calcium (20 electrons). How do the electrons fill?
column28: Fill from the inside out, 2 then 8 then 8: 2 + 8 + 8 = 18, and the last 2 go on the fourth ring. 2, 8, 8, 2.

column9: Which energy level fills first?
column15: The one closest to the nucleus
column16: The one furthest from the nucleus
column17: They all fill at the same time
column28: Electrons fill the level closest to the nucleus first, then move outward.

column9: Valence electrons are the electrons…
column17: That have been lost already
column28: Valence electrons are the ones on the outermost energy level. They decide how an atom reacts.
